Question: How can you create an LLC partnership when your the other partner is in Europe?
Answer: The short answer is, “yes.” The longer answer is that when you say “LLC partnership,” I infer that to mean the entity type is a “limited liability company” (or LLC), and the tax status is “partnership.” If that’s what you mean, then you are absolutely correct. Foreign nationals can have an ownership interest in US-based companies, although for entities classified as “S-Corp” for tax treatment purposes, foreign nationals are not entitled to own such entities. The penalty is relatively harmless: The company looses its S-Corp tax treatment status, and reverts to “partnership.” We do this sort of thing all the time for clients and new companies. Learn more here: Form a Limited Liability Company (LLC) | Law 4 Small Business, P.C. (L4SB). Just as an aside, foreign nationals can also have an ownership interest in an Anonymous LLC. The tax issues and everything else are exactly the same. Learn more here: Maintain Your Privacy With an Anonymous LLC | Law 4 Small Business, P.C. (L4SB). Thank you. Larry.

Question: Does opening an LLC require legal help?
Answer: Do you need legal help to open an LLC? There are really two answers to this. Here’s why I say this: Somewhere around 50% of our firm’s revenue comes from “partnership disputes.” These disputes are worse than bad divorces (i.e. think, The War of the Roses (1989) - IMDb). They involve expensive litigation, and our clients can spend $50k or more trying to save the company or seek damages from bad actors. The worst disputes seem to happen because the LLC (or Corporation) wasn’t properly put together. The formation papers are a mess. For a LLC, the Operating Agreement is sloppy or a poorly-fitting template. Here’s the problem: When you’re just starting out, it makes sense to spend as little money as possible and the appeal of the non-lawyers (many responding to this question) is alluring. However, if you think your company will have any chance of success, the more successful, the bigger a target it becomes — and the greater a chance for disputes (with the IRS, the State and/or partners). I wrote a recent blog article about “Bad Operating Agreements” (See What is a Bad Operating Agreement? | Law 4 Small Business, P.C. (L4SB)). You’d be surprised how many problems can creep up. The expensive problems are problems that will bit you years later, that are hard to predict: IRS audit, partnership dispute, or a partner dying and having to deal with an estate. We wrote an expert system to build a high-quality, highly customized Operating Agreement — for $29.95. It’s the first in the business, as far as I can tell. You can learn more by going here: The Couture Operating Agreement for LLC's | Law 4 Small Business, P.C. (L4SB). Thank you. Larry.

Question: How do I add an additional owner to an LLC?
Answer: This is such an easy question to ask, but difficult to answer. The reason is, the answer depends on a lot of different factors, including (but not limited to), how many owners it currently has, it’s tax status, how the additional owner is joining the LLC (i.e. buying or gifted ownership), and if buying, how is he or she buying the ownership (i.e. cash immediately, promissory note, etc), do the existing owners want the ability to “claw back” the ownership under certain circumstances, etc. Note, too, that change in ownership structure can trigger an updated Beneficial Ownership Interest report to FinCEN under the Corporate Transparency Act (for all new companies, formed after 1/1/2024, and all pre-existing companies formed prior to 1/1/2024, in 1/1/2025 and after). Therefore, the best answer of course is to hire a business attorney to help you. The second best answer is to use our expert system to help you with this. We wrote it, to help people understand the issues. It’s free, takes about 3–7 minutes (depending on the complexity of your setup), and anonymous. You can access it from here: What Do I Need to Do, In Order to Change the Ownership Structure of an Existing Company? Good luck to you. Larry. PS> We also wrote an expert system to help answer questions about the Beneficial Ownership Interest reporting requirements, if you’re interested. Again, it’s free, anonymous and takes 3–10 minutes (depending on complexity of your company). Here’s the link: Reporting for Beneficial Ownership Information (BOI) under the Corporate Transparency Act (CTA)
